clinicalPearls: The commonest scarring alopecia in women of African descent, producing progressive symmetrical hair loss that begins at the crown or vertex and spreads centrifugally
It is often insidious and initially asymptomatic, though itching, tenderness or tingling may occur and patients may notice reduced density before frank baldness
The affected scalp becomes smooth and shiny with loss of follicular ostia, confirming a scarring process
Trichoscopy characteristically shows a peripilar grey-white halo around emerging hairs together with follicular dropout
Proposed associations include traumatic hairstyling with traction, heat and chemical relaxers, genetic factors including PADI3 gene variants, and possibly metabolic factors
Early diagnosis matters because arresting the inflammation can preserve remaining follicles, whereas scarred zones cannot regrow
Management combines gentle hair-care modification with anti-inflammatory therapy such as topical or intralesional corticosteroids and, at times, oral anti-inflammatory antibiotic-class agents
reference.pathophysiology: Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia is a primary scarring alopecia in which chronic inflammation and premature desquamation of the inner root sheath lead to follicular destruction and perifollicular fibrosis, beginning at the vertex and expanding outward. A genetic predisposition, including variants in the PADI3 gene that affect hair-shaft formation, appears to interact with hairdressing practices that impose traction, heat and chemical trauma. The final common pathway is irreversible loss of follicular stem cells with replacement by fibrous tracts.
additionalDifferentials: Androgenetic alopecia, which is non-scarring with preserved ostia
additionalInvestigations: Trichoscopy showing peripilar white or grey halos and loss of ostia
Scalp biopsy from an active margin confirming perifollicular fibrosis and premature inner-root-sheath desquamation
Assessment for coexisting traction alopecia at the margins
Screening for metabolic associations where clinically indicated
redFlags: Pustules, marked inflammation or tufting suggesting folliculitis decalvans or secondary infection
Rapidly expanding loss threatening extensive permanent baldness
Features suggesting discoid lupus that need systemic evaluation
reference.prognosis: Progression can be halted or slowed with early anti-inflammatory treatment and modification of hair care, but established scarred areas will not regrow, so late presentation carries a poorer cosmetic outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking early central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia for androgenetic alopecia and missing the scarring process
Delaying biopsy until the scalp is burnt out, when little can be done
Neglecting to address damaging hairstyling practices
Overlooking a superimposed traction alopecia at the hairline
